# Copper July 2011 

- Momentum from the end of June rally on hopes that a Greek tragedy would be avoided carried through into early July and indeed, through most of the month amid generally positive sentiment.  Certainly, July was not without the odd negative data point to give the bears something to growl about, but hopes for a workable resolution to Greece’s debt problems, in addition the bulls’ old favourite, supply problems, kept prices well supported throughout month. 

- Copper markets read the script back in May and duly fell in line with the old adage to sell in May, so perhaps the price rally this month should not have been expected.  As we noted last month, the way economic events unfold over the coming weeks will give direction to prices, in particular, the outcome of talks in the US to raise its debt ceiling. Meanwhile, should Chinese imports continue their improvement from this month, prices ought to be supported at current levels at least, while the potential for further supply disruptions adds upside risk.  We reiterate our view that prices will be fundamentally supported in the second half of the year and have kept our fourth quarter forecast of $10,000/t intact, while raising our estimate of Q3 prices to $9700/t. 

- The tumultuous economic backdrop has had very little real impact on demand for refined material, with the main drag on consumption simply being consumers winding down activity ahead of their summer shutdowns for care and maintenance.  Apparent consumption in China should be boosted in the coming months from an upturn in imports, although downside risks hover in the background in the shape of rampant Chinese inflation. 

- July spot concentrate market activity played out much in the same way as June did, with trading conditions remaining exceedingly quiet.  In terms of fresh sales from the mining sector there were a couple of transactions of note, firstly from Canada and then more latterly from Australia.  And, despite there being a number of weeks between these trades, the level of terms achieved were fairly stable over this period i.e. in the low 60s & 6s, which is a reduction of around $13/t & 1.3c/lb from last month’s rates.

## Market Developments 

**Prices climb despite uncertain economic backdrop** Momentum from the end of June rally on hopes that a Greek tragedy would be avoided carried through into early July and indeed, through most of the month amid generally positive sentiment.  Certainly, July was not without the odd negative data point to give the bears something to growl about, but hopes for a workable resolution to Greece’s debt problems, in addition the bulls’ old favourite, supply problems, kept prices edging higher until well into the second half of the month.  Just as talk was turning to the return of $10,000/t copper, stocks snapped their declining streak, while negative economic data stoked fears of a sharper-than-expected slowdown in China to drag cash quotes lower as the month drew to a close. 

**Hope then (debt) relief drives early rally** As we were putting the finishing touches to our report this time a month ago it looked as though copper would end the month where it started, at around the US$9000/t mark, before news of a deal to roll over Greek debt boosted market sentiment and lifted prices.  This was quickly followed by further gains on hopes that the Greek parliament would vote through austerity measures that are a precondition for a second Greek bailout.  As European politicians wrangled over the best solution to Greece’s troubles, lawmakers across the Atlantic were discussing their own debt problems as the US seeks to address its debt ceiling.  Against this uncertain economic backdrop, it was perhaps surprising that copper started the month so buoyantly but fundamental factors also played their part in the metal’s rally. 

**Fundamental factors also lend support** It was not simply economic news that was driving the price, however, as supply problems, declining inventories and a relatively weak dollar also underpinned the advance.  Indeed, mine production came to the fore after a series of strikes hit the headlines, while to compound matters, unusually severe winter storms also hit output in Chile.  Prices peaked at $9818.5/t on 19<sup>th</sup> of the month before beginning to dip the following day on a combination of increasing in LME inventories and a firmer dollar against both the euro and sterling. Interestingly, the relative strength of the dollar cannot really be attributed to movements in copper price levels as the dollar strengthened against the euro but weakened relative to sterling, for example, over the course of the month. 

**Unexpected strikes take toll on supply** This month we have had a rash of unexpected strike actions at copper mines, some of which remain ongoing.  BHP-B’s 57.5%-held Chilean subsidiary, Minera Escondida, has been completely shut down since Friday July 22<sup>nd</sup> and has now declared force majeure as 2350 union members strike over what they consider to be unpaid bonuses and other outstanding issues.  Likely output lost there will be in the region of 2.5-3.0kt/d.  Also

in Chile, national company Codelco suffered a one-day strike across its divisions on July 11th, costing a possible 5kt copper. Unions there are concerned that the government will attempt to privatise the copper business as it is doing across other sectors. Both these issues came outside the labour contract re-negotiation periods, which is unusual in Chile. However, the fact that the unions at the Codelco sites fear for their jobs because of the threat of privatisation indicates a longer-term potential for unrest. This 24-hour action came only weeks after contractors disrupted output at El Teniente in June for almost a week. Elsewhere, the market “lost” almost 12kt due to an eight-day, out-of-contract strike at Freeport’s Grasberg, which began on the 4th. This issue for the moment has been resolved, but proper negotiations regarding the renewal of the current two-year contract, which ends this October, are now underway. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2011 Page 2 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Striking the right balance on disruptions** It was interesting that supply issues, and strikes in particular, provided so much support to sentiment through the month as our analysis of disruptions so far this year reveals that worker discontent has had only a modest impact. In fact, as the chart below highlights, technical problems and slow ramp up have had a much bigger impact so far this year, accounting for 31% and 38% of lost output respectively. Meanwhile, strikes have accounted for only 6% of the 529kt of lost output in 2011, although clearly the ongoing strike at Escondida does have the potential to add to this figure. That workers downing tools has played a relatively minor role in disruptions does not come as a particular surprise to us given the number of contract negotiations that were completed last year, although as the disruption at El Teniente revealed this could be something of a red herring. Indeed, it was subcontractors and not salaried workers who brought Codelco’s operations there to a halt. #### **Global supply disruptions in 2011** Total = 529kt

**Taking stock of inventory movements** At the same time as Southern hemisphere winter chills of worker discontent were lifting prices, LME stocks which

had peaked for the year at 477,925t on 9<sup>th</sup> June and had begun to decline from the end of that month, continued to fall, hitting a monthly low of 461,275 on 5<sup>th</sup> July and remaining at similar levels for around the next ten days.  The rise which followed was initially gentle, but picked up pace after inflows into Chicago and New Orleans, which could easily have been viewed as marking an end to drawdowns from LME warehouses.  However, we understand that the inflows into these locations were more to do with the movement of metal from off to on warrant and because of the various incentives that are being offered to house material than a reflection of underlying demand. Indeed, LME stocks in both Europe and Asia ebbed lower through the month of July and as such, the increase in inventories that has been seen should not be viewed as a signal for weakening demand and thus, softer prices. 

Chinese exchange stock levels have been increasing week by week through most of July, up from c.81kt at the end of June to 112kt on 22<sup>nd</sup> July following on from their steady decline from just under 180kt in mid-March.  Declining Chinese inventories, both on exchange and those in bonded warehouses, have been underpinning the belief that Chinese imports will spark into life in the second half of the year and in doing so drive prices higher again.  However, the increase in SHFE stocks failed to dent this belief, with the movement simply viewed as stocks moving out of bonded warehouses and onto exchange, with bonded stocks now estimated at 250-300kt.  Meanwhile, COMEX stocks were broadly unchanged through July. 

**Chinese premia remain strong despite stock rise** As we noted above, looking at stock movements alone does not tell the whole story, as premia remaining at elevated levels is more instructive in this case.  In China, for example, premia stand at around $100/t, at similar levels to last month, pointing to steady demand even as we move into the seasonally quiet period and despite SHFE stock levels climbing through July.  In fact, latest Chinese data points to slightly firmer end use consumption, with semis output posting their best gain (by our calculations) this year, although there are several caveats to the data, some of which we discussed here last month.  Significantly though, the underlying trend of both semis output and apparent consumption are on an upward trajectory, with calculations boosted by a sharp improvement in imports into China following favourable arbitrage conditions.  In addition to the still relatively low stock levels, this should point to further improvements in imports, and consumption of refined metal, in the months to come.

## Consumption 

The tumultuous economic backdrop has had very little real impact on demand for refined material, with the main drag on consumption simply being consumers winding down activity ahead of their summer shutdowns for care and maintenance.  Apparent consumption in China should be boosted in the coming months from an upturn in imports, although downside risks hover in the background in the shape of rampant Chinese inflation. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Crisis averted** Greece’s debt problems continued to plague financial and commodity markets in July although by and large the European economy has endured little actual impact from the ongoing crisis.  Indeed, industrial activity continues to drive key industrial centres, although a significant volume of this output is destined for outside Europe, while consumer reticence to spend remains the drag on economic activity overall. 

Eurozone industrial production rose 0.1% month-over-month in May, far less than the expected rise of 0.5%.  Production of energy and capital goods increased by 0.9% and 0.6%, respectively, while durable and non-durable consumer goods, however, fell by 0.5% and 0.4%, respectively.  There is some conflict within the indicators as to where IP may be heading in the next few months: the preliminary PMI for July is down to 50.35, a fraction above the expansionary threshold, while the new orders index dropped to 47.6, suggesting that orders are contracting.  This would suggest that Q3 will be a very poor quarter for European IP.  However, industrial new orders rose by 3.6% month on month in May and by 15.5% year on year, well above market expectations and contradicting the PMI number. 

**Eurozone retail sales** fell 1.1% month-over-month in May.  The largest decline since April 2010 was partially attributed to a 2.8% drop in retail sales in Germany.  Year-over-year, retail sales dropped 1.9%.  The data reaffirm that

eurozone growth has slowed appreciably since Q1.  Given the regional fiscal outlook, there does not seem to be much reason for Europeans to increase spending any time soon. 

**Interest rake hike confirms view of H2 slowdown…** We have always said that we expect a slowdown in cathode demand in the second half of the year and the recent interest rate hike from the European Central Bank has confirmed our view.  For now though, cathode consumption remains reasonable, even if softer than a month ago as firms ease down production ahead of summer shutdowns.  The underlying trend remains firm, however, with year-on-year comparisons remaining healthy, while it is wire rod that continues to lead end use demand. 

**… as construction outlook remains gloomy** The Euro construction PMI fell in June to 46 from 47 in May, revealing that construction orders are falling once again in Europe, having increased during Q1 of this year.  Housing activity in particular showed a steep drop, reflecting the caution of households in the face of slowing economic growth.  We had previously been expecting Eurozone residential construction to grow in 2011 for the first time in 4 years, but the latest data places doubt on that assumption.  In all, total construction will more than likely to contract in 2011 and 2012. 

**Auto output to expand by 4.6% in western Europe in 2011** The economic recovery in western Europe has been distinctly varied from one country to another.  In auto production, a similar trend is occurring.  Following year-on-year growth of 13% in 2010, output in Germany is expanding solidly once again, driven by high levels of export demand.  In Italy and Spain, by contrast, production looks likely to contract this year, with a large part of the decline attributable to weakness in domestic demand for new cars – Spanish car registrations fell by 31% year on year in June.  We expect auto production in western Europe to grow by 4.6% in 2011, down from 10.9% in 2010, but still well above trend growth. The majority of this will come from Germany, where output is forecast to increase by 9.6% to 6.5M vehicles.  In 2012, growth across the region will be slightly slower at 4.5%, as much improved output in Italy is offset by slower growth in Germany and the UK. 

**Full year growth estimate maintained at 2.3%** As we have noted above, despite a first half that has exceeded expectations, our view has always been that activity will ease back in the second half of the year.  We see no reason to change this, particularly given the uncertain economic backdrop.  As such, we maintain our view of a 2.3% expansion in Western European refined demand this year, with a further easing back in 2012.

### **Americas** 

**Politics and macrodata weighing down the US** As the political situation over raising the debt ceiling continues to hog the headlines in the USA, various industrial data add w

eight to the anecdotal evidence of an early summer decline in activity and copper demand. In the autos sector, total vehicle production slipped by 6.6% in April to June from the previous quarter. Many assembly lines of Japanese producers in particular in the US were forced to run at reduced operating rates due to a shortage of parts, following the March earthquake in Japan. This situation has abated, though. Toyota commented in June that it expects to return to full capacity at all of its North American plants by September – two-thirds of its plants returned to 100% in June – and will focus on making up for production lost earlier in the year. However, the deterioration of the US economic performance makes for a great deal of uncertainty whether the demand is there to meet increased production volumes. The Conference Board survey showed 3.1% of US households were planning to buy a new car in the next six months, down from 4.5% in April. In the US housing market, sentiment was initially buoyed with the release that new starts rose a more-than-expected 14.6% month-on-month in June to an annual rate of 629,000. This is a five-month high and is 16.7% higher than June 2010. But the surge is likely to be a “one-off” event, as builders took advantage of better weather to start projects that had been delayed earlier in the year. While the increase remains a welcome development, continued decline in home prices and delays in processing foreclosures means it may take years to clear the market of distressed properties. Building permits, which measure future building activity, rose by 2.5% m-o-m. Existing-home sales fell 0.8% (month-onmonth) in June to an annual rate of 4.77 million. This is a seven-month low. The decline was due to an unusual increase in contract cancellations. Year-over-year, home sales were down 8.8%. Meanwhile, US consumer confidence levels fell again last month and now stands at its lowest level since last November (58.5). No doubt the lingering high unemployment levels are partly responsible, with June’s rate standing at 9.2%. **Summer slowdown appearing in industrials** At the metals level, it looks as though the general economic environment is taking some toll on production and deliveries. Copper rod output slipped a little in May to 107.7kt from April’s 110.4kt, according to data provided by the American Bureau of Metals Statistics. Meanwhile, data from the Copper and Brass Servicecenter Association also show a tail-off in shipments from the first quarter. During that period, the CBSA’s members shipped an average of 10.4kt/m, but this fell to 9.4kt for April and May. Shipments of brass products at mill level show a strong first two months of the year, as per other sectors of the copper business, but data lags significantly and will probably reflect the declines noted elsewhere. #### **US Copper and Brass Servicecenter shipments (kt)** 12

**Tecnofil close to completing Sherburne acquisition** Privately-owned Peruvian copper and alloy rod and shapes producer, Tecnofil, will complete its acquisition of Sherburne Metals of Sherburne, NY by the end of this month for an undisclosed sum. Sherburne has not been in operation for over a year and has been actively looking for a buyer. It has two UpCast rod lines available: a 30kt/a capacity unit that has been in operation since 1983, and a 15kt/a line that was installed in 1999. Tecnofil is an experienced UpCast user, with three lines operating since 1997 at its Lima facility. It currently has 22kt/a copper rod capacity from two lines and a further 7.2kt/a brass alloys rod capacity from the third; the company bought all these units second-hand, from prior rod producers in Mexico, Venezuela and the Philippines. Tecnofil intends to re-start the Sherburne rod lines in-situ, rather than dismantle them and move them to Peru. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2011 Page 7 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Chile’s CCC rod expansion application “inadmissible”** Nexans subsidiary, Colada Continua Chilena (CCC), has had its application for an increase in capacity declared inadmissible for evaluation by the government’s Environmental Assessment Service. CCC has been preparing documents seeking approval for two discrete 20kt/a UpCast oxygen free rod lines to be installed at its Quilicura, Santiago site since November last year, and has made two applications this year. However, it appears that the application has failed to pass the relatively new Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA) for as-yet undisclosed reasons, and the company has yet to state publicly whether or not it will try again. CCC was formed in the late-1980s as a partnership between Madeco, Cobre Cerillos (Cocesa, a Phelps Dodge subsidiary since 1968 with its own but antiquated rod line) and cable-maker Elaboradora de Cobre Viсa del Mar (Covisa). It has been operating its own Contirod line at Quilicura to make ETP grade rod since 1989 and has since expanded the initial 45kt/a capacity unit to one with 74kt/a capacity. Cocesa, now owned by General Cable following its acquisition of Phelps Dodge International Corp, and Covisa continue as partners in CCC (and as rod offtake customers for their own wire-drawing lines) along with Nexans, which took over Madeco’s rod and wire-making facilities across South America earlier this decade. The two new UpCast lines represented an investment of US$8M, with the first line coming into operation within seven months of receiving all the necessary permits from the government. The second line would become available within two or three years after the first, dependent upon market requirements. ### **China** **Economic data leave plenty of questi

ons unanswered** Plenty of economic releases caught the headlines this month, with most pointing to strong economic growth for the time being but worryingly, inflation also surprised on the upside. Second quarter GDP came in ahead of expectations at 9.5% in the second quarter, while industrial output reaccelerated to 15.1% growth in June, although the sharp rise in inflation to 6.4% underscored the fact that further tightening measures might be required from Chinese authorities.  This could be easily have been countered by the release of flash PMI data, which pointed to a contraction in manufacturing output in the months to come, if it were not for the fact that this has historically been a poor indicator of things to come.  Overall then, the big question of whether the Chinese central bank has come to the end of its tightening cycle is far from answered by the mixed set of data released over the past month. 

Over the past few months many of the key indicators of demand for copper have been positive, with high premia, declining stocks and a favourable arbitrage all pointing to an increase in imports into China in the second half of the year. In the first half, imports of refined metal have, of course, massively disappointed and were down by 30% on the first six months of 2010, although the latest figure for June did at least bring a halt to the month-on-month declines that we had been seeing since April.  At the same time, the pace of exports has slowed sharply to a halt, in line with firmer domestic demand and the favourable arbitrage that we mentioned above, although having been open for the past few months this window has now close and importing material has become relatively more costly than domestic purchases once again. 

**Rising imports to boost apparent consumption in H2** With bonded warehouse stocks at the 250-300kt level, there is little room to move here as most of the material still there is tied up in financing deals and even if SHFE stocks have edged up a little over the course of the past month or so, they are still at relatively low levels.  Meanwhile, with semis production posting its best gain (by our calculations) this year in June this would suggest that demand for copper is beginning to build up some momentum, even as we are heading into the seasonally quiet summer months.  As such, these factors ought to suggest that imports will continue to improve in the coming months to add what has so far been a decent year for refined copper production and thus lift apparent consumption in the second half of the year.  The risks to this are of course that credit tightening measures result in a hard landing for the Chinese economy, although given the importance of the infrastructure spend to copper consumption, even in the face of a sharp slowdown in industrial activity overall, demand should be sheltered at least to a degree. 

**Chinese published construction numbers surprise on the upside** Given that housing starts had massively o

utpaced completions in the past two years, it was implicit that China has a large number of buildings sitting idle and officially not complete. But instead of the weak growth in starts we expected, construction numbers continue to be strong, with starts up by 24% year on year in the first half of 2011, continuing to outpace the 13% growth in completions. It turns out that a large part of social housing is actually included in published statistics, despite having been told to the contrary earlier in the year. Of the annual social housing target of 10m units, 50% had been started by the end of June. This is why the published numbers have continued to hold up so well. By year end, 4m of the 10m should have been completed. Meanwhile, the State Council has announced that purchase restrictions will be extended into the tier 2 cities, where prices are rising rapidly. The move indicates that there will be no let-up in restrictions across real estate within the next year. **Automotive market in consolidation mode** 2011 is a year of consolidation for the Chinese auto industry after two years of rapid expansion in vehicle sales and production. Although disruptions caused by the Japan earthquake have had an impact on Chinese vehicle production, the slowdown has primarily been caused by the Chinese consumer. Vehicle sales began to slow after the expiration of incentive schemes at the turn of the year, and policies introduced in some major cities to limit new vehicle registrations have not helped. In addition, higher fuel prices have dented consumer sentiment towards buying a car. As a result, total vehicle sales growth slowed to 3.8% year on year during the first half of the year, down from 33% in 2010. As a result of this relatively sluggish pace of demand by Chinese standards, we do not expect vehicle production growth in excess of 5% this year. ### **Japan** **Japanese economy bouncing back** Economic and industrial activity is slowly returning to normal in Japan and this is being reflected in healthy gains in industrial output, although clearly some of the month-on-month gains are a little flattering. Industrial production rose by 5.7% month-over-month in May, with the gain primarily down to an increase in passenger car and truck production, while the general machinery and chemical sectors also assisted in the rise. According to forecasts contained in the government data, production is expected to have risen by 5.3% in June and by 0.5% in July. The

Japan Tankan Survey showed a sharp decline in sentiment in the second quarter.  A big drop in overall sentiment was expected since more than 70% of last quarter’s survey was collected before the March earthquake.  On the plus side, the survey showed that businesses plan to increase capital spending by 4.2% in the current fiscal year, which began in April. 

**Shipments maintain solid pace** Despite the tumultuous backdrop and the collapse in key end use sectors, overall shipments to the wire and cable sector have held up very impressively.  Shipments posted a fresh year-on-year gain in June, which leaves first half shipments up by just under 2%, which is pretty impressive in the circumstances.  The construction of temporary housing came to the rescue, although shipments to this sector are beginning to ease back after sharp growth in April and May, while the telecommunication sector has also benefitted from reconstruction efforts after a very weak first quarter.  Unsurprisingly, automotive shipments are the laggard, although these are expected to tick higher as car production returns to normal in the final part of the year. 

**Construction still bumping along the bottom** The disaster in Japan has provided a short term boost to shipments of wire and cable to the construction sector, but overall building activity in Japan remains far from healthy.  Housing starts in May increased by 6.4% year on year to 63,726 units, but the figure was still the 3rd lowest for May on record, underlining the fact that recovery has a long way to go.  Meanwhile, there is a huge amount of regional variation, with starts in the Kanto region around Tokyo up by 24%, in contrast to the decline of 30% in the quake-hit Tohoku and 16% in and around Osaka in the West.  The data suggest that reconstruction is still someway off for the quake-hit areas and confirms our view of no real benefit from reconstruction efforts (aside from the building of temporary homes) in 2011. 

**Auto sector steps up a gear** Natural disasters in March triggered a collapse in Japanese automotive output as supply chains were severely disrupted as output declined by close to 60% year on year in March and April, and by 31% in May. The damage and resulting disruptions were so extensive that automakers were not initially expecting to return to normal output until the end of the year.  However, supply chains have recovered faster than many expected, meaning that Japanese production should be near full capacity before the end of the third quarter.  Producers are planning to hire additional workers during the autumn, in an attempt to recover lost output, but the earlier disruptions were so severe that we expect total vehicle production for 2011 will be down by 7% from 2010.  Pent-up export and domestic demand should ensure a solid rebound in 2012, with growth of 12.6%.

**Freeport boosts NA copper output in Q2** Away from the labour-related issues at its Indonesian operations which, as mentioned lost almost 12kt lost copper in concentrate output in early July, Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold had a largely successful second quarter at its North American operations, boosting sales by 14.5% vs Q2 2010.  Higher production at both Morenci and Miami, plus a re-start of mining and milling at the Chino, New Mexico sulphide operations after a two-year closure period, all contributed to output of 142kt vs 119kt and sales of 150kt vs 131kt during the two comparable quarters.  At Morenci, Freeport has now completed its ramp up in mining rates to 635kt/d ore and milling to 50kt/d.  This should bring about a three-fold increase in copper in concentrate output this year to 90-100kt from just 30kt in 2010, and allow output from this route to level out at between 70-80kt/a over the long term.  Copper from the SxEw route will also increase from the 200kt levels seen last year and projected for this year to c.250kt in 2012 and to c.290kt for the following four years.  At Chino, Freeport expects planned mining and milling rates to be achieved by the end of 2013 after the ongoing US$150M investment in equipment and mill refurbishment, and copper in concentrate output of 10kt this year, building to 60kt by 2014; meanwhile, metal via the SxEw route should increase to 40kt this year from just 15kt in 2010, building up to 65-70kt/a through to 2017. 

At its South American operations, Freeport began production from the newly commissioned stacking and leaching facilities as its transitions from oxide to sulphide ores at its 51%-held El Abra property in Chile.  El Abra has produced on average 160kt/a of SxEw copper over the last four years, but from the second half of this year all output (at the same tonnes rate) will come from predominantly sulphide ores.  Of the proposed US$725M capital investment for this change through to 2015, roughly US$565M for the initial phase of the project will be spent on equipment that will be completed this year.  There is also and ongoing PFS to determine the potential for a large-scale milling plant to improve recoveries and increase sulphides processed.  At its 53.56%-held C

Copper Monthly Update 

Meanwhile in the USA, Glencore took up a private placement of 5 million common shares in exploration company PolyMet Mining Corp for US$10M; it also acquired a further 9.2M shares in PolyMet from Cliffs Erie LLC at a price of US$1.4233/share.  Glencore now owns a 17.89% stake in PolyMet, and has rights to increase its holding to 24.95% by taking similar future actions.  PolyMet controls 100% of the NorthMet polymetallic orebody in the Mesabi Range area of north eastern Minnesota, as well as 100% of the Erie processing plant once utilized by steelmaker LTV.  The company intends to bring NorthMet into operation in a phased approach, initially producing a bulk concentrate for sale to third parties but then, in Phase II, isolating copper as a single, higher-grade concentrate amounting to 36kt/a Cu contained, leaving Ni-Co hydroxide and precious metals precipitates as discrete products. 

**Miheevsky remains on track for 2013 commissioning, 2014 start** This month Finnish technology supplier Outotec confirmed the design and delivery of a new, €60M copper concentrator for the Miheevsky project belonging to Russian Copper Co (RCC), located in Chelyabinsk, southwest Russia.  The equipment includes flotation and dewatering units with a dozen TankCell® 300 flotation machines (said by Outotec to be the world’s largest), Proscon® automation, instrumentation, electrification, spare parts and training as well as site supervision services for installation and start-up. The equipment deliveries will take place during 2012 and 2013

. The Miheevsky concentrator is planning to treat 18Mt/a of copper ore and it is expected to be commissioned by the end of 2013. We show this mine coming into initial production during H2 2014, and building to steady-state operations of 60-65kt/a copper in concentrate by 2015. In late May, RCC placed a €200M order with Metso for a primary gyratory crusher, three cone crushers, two SAG mills, three screens and three ball mills for the Miheevsky project, including a six-year service contract covering on-site personnel training and parts supply. The main equipment component of that contract was valued at €75M. **Uzbek’s Almalyk in €30M acid recovery spend** OJSC Almalyk Mining & Metallurgical Company (AMMC) also ordered equipment from Outotec this month, this time valued at €30M. The company will receive gas cleaning and sulfuric acid plant technology with a view to reducing SO2 emissions by recovering 0.5Mt/a of sulphuric acid. AMMC, whose production of copper in concentrate has fallen in recent year from 90-100kt/a during the earlier part of this decade to 7585kt/a since 2007, hopes to return output to 100kt/a on a regular basis from 2015, and this environmental protection equipment constitutes one part of this plan. **QuadraFNX to more than double production with Sierra Gorda** Early this month, Vancouver-based QuadraFNX Mining Ltd obtained environmental impact assessment approval for its Sierra Gorda project in Region II, northern Chile. With that it passed a US$1Bn EPCM contract along to Fluor Corp for the mine’s planned processing plant. Sierra Gorda, owned 55% by QuadraFNX, 31.5% by Sumitomo Corp. and 13.5% by Sumitomo Metal Mining Co., is now planning to start pre-stripping next year to bring the project into production by mid-2014. Long-term average annual output of 210220kt copper in concentrates is expected by 2017. QuadraFNX’s current annual copper output from five properties amounts to c.95-100kt in both concentrate and SxEw forms. **Newcrest plans for Cadia East progress as scheduled** Australian gold-copper producer, Newcrest, hit copper output targets during Q2 and has kept the investment programme at Cadia Hill to schedule. The A$1.9Bn Cadia East project in New South Wales should ensure copper in concentrate output increases from the current annual rate of 25-30kt/a to 40kt in 2013 and then to 80kt/a for the following decade. This quarter, Cadia Hill produced 5.8kt copper contained in 30.8k dmt concentrate, with 12-month data being 23.4kt and 121k dmt, respectively.
